note: The counted exception to fill-empty-only: every theme here exists in the source with a band-suffixed description (the documented content debt); this promotion replaces exactly those rows with five authored sentences per theme. The normaliser refuses any other target. Track names, prefixes, codes, credentials and transfer checks are untouched.

themes.description: Establishing who is affected before deciding what they need.

bands.K–2: After a storm story, say who was affected before saying what they need.
bands.3–5: Estimate how many people in a story town were affected by a flood, and say how you counted.
bands.6–8: Produce an affected-population estimate for a described situation with its method stated, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce an affected-population estimate with its method stated.
bands.11–12: Produce an affected-population estimate for a real or exercise situation with its method, and defend it to the coordination body.

themes.description: Rapid assessment that reports its own uncertainty rather than hiding it.

bands.K–2: Guess how many children are in the playground, then say how sure you are.
bands.3–5: Make a quick count of something and give a lowest and highest number you are confident of.
bands.6–8: Publish a rapid assessment of a described situation with explicit confidence bounds, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Publish an assessment with explicit confidence bounds.
bands.11–12: Publish a real or exercise rapid assessment with confidence bounds and record how the bounds were used by decision-makers.

themes.description: Counting a population in motion, where every method has a known failure.

bands.K–2: Try to count people walking past a door and say why it is hard.
bands.3–5: Count a moving group two different ways and say what each way missed.
bands.6–8: Compare two counting methods on a described moving population and state what each misses, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Compare two counting methods and state what each misses.
bands.11–12: Compare two counting methods on a real or exercise population in motion, state what each misses, and recommend one for the setting.

themes.theme: The data the community already has
themes.description: The data the community already holds, and why it is usually collected again.

bands.K–2: Before counting the class, ask whether the teacher already has a register.
bands.3–5: Find data a school or town already has before collecting it again.
bands.6–8: Find existing local data for a described context and use it rather than duplicating it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find existing local data and use it rather than duplicating it.
bands.11–12: Find and use existing local data in a real assessment, and document what the community was not asked again.

themes.theme: Assessment fatigue and the harm of it
themes.description: Assessment fatigue: the harm of repeatedly asking people to describe their worst month.

bands.K–2: Say how it feels to be asked the same hard question again and again.
bands.3–5: Shorten a long survey so it asks less of people, and say what you gave up.
bands.6–8: Redesign an assessment to reduce burden and state what you gave up, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Redesign an assessment to reduce burden and state what you gave up.
bands.11–12: Redesign a real assessment with the people who answer it, reduce the burden, and state to the funder what was given up.

themes.description: Disaggregation that changes a decision, rather than disaggregation as a compliance box.

bands.K–2: Sort class data by something that changes a decision — like who needs a bigger chair.
bands.3–5: Split a dataset by age or gender and find one decision it changes.
bands.6–8: Disaggregate one dataset and identify a decision it changes, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Disaggregate one dataset and identify a decision it changes.
bands.11–12: Disaggregate a real dataset, identify the decision it changes, and get that decision made.

themes.description: The gap between what is needed and what is fundable, stated rather than absorbed.

bands.K–2: Make a list of what a class needs and a list of what it was given, side by side.
bands.3–5: Write what a story town needs and what the money on offer would pay for, side by side.
bands.6–8: Produce both lists side by side for one described context, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce both lists side by side for one context.
bands.11–12: Produce both lists for a real context and put the gap in writing to the funder.

themes.theme: Saying the need is smaller than assumed
themes.description: Reporting a need smaller than expected, which is professionally harder than the reverse.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult honestly when a problem turned out smaller than everyone thought.
bands.3–5: Write a note saying a need is smaller than expected, and why that is hard to say.
bands.6–8: Write the finding and the covering note for a described smaller-than-expected need, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the finding and the covering note.
bands.11–12: Write and send a real finding that a need is smaller than assumed, with its covering note, and record the response.

themes.description: Assessing during active conflict, where access bias is the dominant error.

bands.K–2: Say why you cannot know what is happening in a place you are not allowed to go.
bands.3–5: Say how only being able to visit some places changes what an assessment finds.
bands.6–8: State the access bias in one described assessment and its likely direction, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State the access bias in one assessment and its likely direction.
bands.11–12: State the access bias in a real assessment, its direction, and how the report accounts for it.

themes.description: Publishing something that disappoints the organisation that paid for it.

bands.K–2: Say how to tell someone their idea did not work as well as they hoped.
bands.3–5: Write how you would tell the people who paid for a project that it found something they did not want.
bands.6–8: Draft the publication and the conversation preceding it for a described disappointing assessment, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Draft the publication and the conversation preceding it.
bands.11–12: Publish a real assessment that disappoints its funder, having had the conversation first, and record what changed.

themes.description: What the cluster system coordinates, and what it does not.

bands.K–2: Say what a group of helpers can decide together and what each must decide alone.
bands.3–5: Say what a coordination group of aid organisations decides, and what it does not.
bands.6–8: Reconstruct a cluster meeting from its minutes and state what was actually decided, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Attend or reconstruct a cluster meeting and state what was actually decided.
bands.11–12: Attend real cluster meetings for a month and report what was decided against what was discussed.

themes.description: A meeting worth attending, and how to make one, or leave one.

bands.K–2: Say what a class meeting must decide, or else it should not happen.
bands.3–5: Redesign a school meeting so it produces one decision.
bands.6–8: Redesign one recurring meeting around a decision it must produce, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Redesign one recurring meeting around a decision it must produce.
bands.11–12: Redesign a real recurring coordination meeting around its decision, run it, and record the change.

themes.description: How duplication happens without anybody intending it.

bands.K–2: Find a job two people in class both did without knowing, and say how it happened.
bands.3–5: Trace how two groups ended up doing the same task without meaning to.
bands.6–8: Trace one real or described duplication to its cause, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace one real duplication to its cause.
bands.11–12: Trace a real duplication in a real response to its cause and propose the coordination fix.

themes.theme: Sharing a beneficiary without sharing a record
themes.description: Sharing that somebody is served without sharing anything about them.

bands.K–2: Say how two helpers could know they both helped the same person without sharing their secrets.
bands.3–5: Design a way for two groups to avoid helping the same person twice without sharing personal details.
bands.6–8: Design a deduplication approach that transmits no personal record, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a deduplication approach that transmits no personal record.
bands.11–12: Design and test a real deduplication approach that transmits no personal record, with the partners who would use it.

themes.theme: Localisation, in practice not in language
themes.description: Localisation as budget, decision rights and risk transfer, not as vocabulary.

bands.K–2: Say who decides and who gets the money when a big group helps a small one.
bands.3–5: Look at a partnership and say who holds the budget, the decisions and the risk.
bands.6–8: Assess one described partnership against budget, decision rights and risk transfer, honestly, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Assess one partnership against those three, honestly.
bands.11–12: Assess a real partnership against the three honestly and put the findings to both partners.

themes.theme: Being the international agency in a local room
themes.description: Being the international agency in a national room, and what that costs the room.

bands.K–2: Say how it feels when a visitor takes over a meeting in your classroom.
bands.3–5: Describe a meeting from the point of view of the people who were there before the visitors.
bands.6–8: Describe one described meeting from the other participants' position, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Describe one meeting from the other participants' position.
bands.11–12: Describe a real meeting from the national participants' position, check it with them, and change how you attend the next one.

themes.description: Handover to a national actor, planned from the start rather than at the end.

bands.K–2: Plan from the start how a helper will hand a job back to the person whose job it is.
bands.3–5: Write a plan for handing a project to a local group, with dates and names.
bands.6–8: Write a handover plan for a described programme with dates and named recipients, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a handover plan with dates and named recipients.
bands.11–12: Write a real handover plan with the national actor, with dates and names, and start it.

themes.description: Consortium bids, who leads, and where the overhead actually lands.

bands.K–2: When groups team up for a prize, say who is in charge and who gets the money.
bands.3–5: Draw where the money goes when several organisations bid together.
bands.6–8: Map the money flow in one described consortium structure, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map the money flow in one consortium structure.
bands.11–12: Map the money flow in a real consortium and show where the overhead actually lands.

themes.theme: Exit as a plan rather than an event
themes.description: Exit as a designed phase with criteria, not an event triggered by a funding date.

bands.K–2: Say how you would know a helper's job was finished, before they start.
bands.3–5: Write the conditions under which a project should end, not just the date.
bands.6–8: Write exit criteria for a described running programme, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write exit criteria for a running programme.
bands.11–12: Write exit criteria for a real running programme and get them adopted by the people who fund it.

themes.description: When coordination itself becomes the obstacle, and saying so.

bands.K–2: Say when too many meetings stop work getting done.
bands.3–5: Find one meeting or rule that costs more than it helps, and say so.
bands.6–8: Identify one described coordination cost that exceeds its benefit and argue it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one coordination cost that exceeds its benefit and argue it.
bands.11–12: Identify a real coordination cost that exceeds its benefit and argue it in the forum that can change it.

themes.description: A complaint mechanism people actually use, which is usually not the one that was built.

bands.K–2: Try using the class suggestion box and say what would stop you.
bands.3–5: Test a school's way of complaining from a pupil's point of view and say what stopped you.
bands.6–8: Test a complaint mechanism from a user's position and report what stopped you, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Test a mechanism from a user's position and report what stopped you.
bands.11–12: Test a real mechanism from a user's position with real users, report what stopped them, and change it.

themes.description: Feedback that changes a programme, and the loop that closes back to the person.

bands.K–2: Give feedback on a class rule and find out whether anything changed and whether you were told.
bands.3–5: Trace one piece of feedback at school to a change and to the person being told.
bands.6–8: Trace one piece of feedback in a described programme to a change and to the person being told, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace one piece of feedback to a change and to the person being told.
bands.11–12: Trace real feedback through a real programme to a change and to the person being told, and fix the loop where it broke.

themes.description: Consent where refusal has a cost, which is most of this sector.

bands.K–2: Ask a younger child properly, so they can really say no.
bands.3–5: Describe how to ask permission when saying no might cost the person something.
bands.6–8: Describe how you would make refusal genuinely available in a described programme, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Describe how you would make refusal genuinely available.
bands.11–12: Make refusal genuinely available in a real programme and record the refusals that followed.

themes.theme: Protection from sexual exploitation and abuse
themes.description: Protection from sexual exploitation and abuse: the standards, the reporting, the obligation.

bands.K–2: Say the rules that keep children safe with adults, and whom you tell if a rule is broken.
bands.3–5: State the rules that protect people from harm by helpers, and how to report.
bands.6–8: State the PSEA standards, your obligations and the reporting route precisely, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State your own obligations and the reporting route precisely.
bands.11–12: State your obligations and the reporting route for a real organisation, and be assessed on them by its safeguarding lead.

themes.description: Reporting a colleague, which is the hardest obligation in the sector.

bands.K–2: Say what you would do if a helper did something wrong, even a helper you like.
bands.3–5: Practise reporting something a friend did wrong, and say who protects you.
bands.6–8: Rehearse a report about a colleague and identify the protection available, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Rehearse the report and identify the protection available to you.
bands.11–12: Rehearse the report under a real organisation's procedure and verify the protection actually exists.

themes.theme: Communicating a decision people will not like
themes.description: Communicating a decision people will not like, without hiding behind a policy.

bands.K–2: Tell the class a decision they will not like, with the reason, without hiding behind 'those are the rules'.
bands.3–5: Deliver an unpopular decision in role with the reasoning and what people can do about it.
bands.6–8: Deliver a difficult decision in role and be critiqued on it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Deliver a difficult decision in role and be critiqued on it.
bands.11–12: Deliver a real difficult decision to the people affected, with reasoning and recourse, and be critiqued afterwards.

themes.theme: Participation that is not a workshop photograph
themes.description: Participation that transfers a decision rather than producing a photograph.

bands.K–2: Let the class decide something real, not just pick a colour.
bands.3–5: Name one decision about a school project that pupils could really make, and let them.
bands.6–8: Identify one decision in a described programme you would genuinely transfer, and to whom, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one decision you would genuinely transfer, and to whom.
bands.11–12: Transfer a real decision in a real programme to the people served, and record what they decided.

themes.theme: Being accountable when you are leaving
themes.description: Accountability while leaving, which is when it is least convenient and most owed.

bands.K–2: Before leaving a group, tell them what you finished and what you did not.
bands.3–5: Write what you would tell the people you helped when your project ends.
bands.6–8: Write the exit communication to the people served by a described programme, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the exit communication to the people served.
bands.11–12: Write and deliver the exit communication for a real programme, and record the questions it drew.

themes.description: Do no harm, examined against a real programme rather than recited.

bands.K–2: Find one way helping could accidentally make something worse, and say how to avoid it.
bands.3–5: Apply 'do no harm' to a school project and find one possible harm.
bands.6–8: Apply the framework to a described programme and find one harm, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Apply the framework to a real programme and find one harm.
bands.11–12: Apply the framework to a real programme with its team, find the harm, and change the programme.

themes.description: What people said they wanted, recorded and set beside what was delivered.

bands.K–2: Ask the class what they wanted and write it next to what they got.
bands.3–5: List what people asked a project for and what the project gave, side by side.
bands.6–8: Produce the two lists for a described programme, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce the two lists for one programme.
bands.11–12: Produce the two lists for a real programme, publish them to the people served, and act on the gap.

themes.description: A logframe you could defend to somebody sceptical, including its assumptions.

bands.K–2: Say what you want to happen, what you will do, and why the doing leads to the happening.
bands.3–5: Draw a chain from what a project does to what it hopes will change, and say what has to be true.
bands.6–8: Defend one described logframe's causal chain under challenge, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Defend one logframe's causal chain under challenge.
bands.11–12: Defend a real logframe's causal chain to a sceptical reviewer and revise its assumptions on the record.

themes.description: Indicators that survive contact with a real context rather than a proposal.

bands.K–2: Pick one way to tell whether a class project worked, and check it actually works.
bands.3–5: Test whether a project's measures still make sense once you see the real place.
bands.6–8: Test three described indicators against field reality and revise them, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Test three indicators against field reality and revise them.
bands.11–12: Test a real programme's indicators in the field, revise them, and submit the revision.

themes.description: Cash versus in-kind: the evidence, and the conditions under which each is right.

bands.K–2: Say when giving money is better than giving things, and when it is not.
bands.3–5: Argue whether a story family should get cash or goods, with reasons.
bands.6–8: Argue the cash-or-in-kind choice for one described context, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Argue the choice for one specific context.
bands.11–12: Argue the choice for a real context with the evidence and the market conditions, to the people deciding.

themes.description: Targeting, and the people the targeting criteria exclude.

bands.K–2: When you decide who gets something, say who is left out and whether that is fair.
bands.3–5: Write who a project's rules leave out and whether that can be defended.
bands.6–8: Identify who a described programme's targeting excludes and whether that is defensible, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify who your targeting excludes and whether that is defensible.
bands.11–12: Identify who a real programme's targeting excludes, test the defence with the excluded, and revise.

themes.description: Monitoring when access is limited, and the bias that introduces.

bands.K–2: Say how you would check on a project you cannot visit, and what you might miss.
bands.3–5: Design a way to monitor a project from far away and name its blind spot.
bands.6–8: Design remote monitoring for a described insecure context and state its blind spot, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design remote monitoring and state its blind spot.
bands.11–12: Design and run remote monitoring for a real programme, state its blind spot, and report it with the results.

themes.description: Changing a programme mid-cycle, and the permission that requires.

bands.K–2: Say how you would ask permission to change a plan halfway, with a reason.
bands.3–5: Write a request to change a school project halfway, with the evidence for it.
bands.6–8: Draft a revision request for a described programme with the evidence for it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Draft a revision request with the evidence for it.
bands.11–12: Draft and submit a real revision request with the evidence, and record the decision.

themes.description: Reporting failure to a donor, which is the report that improves the sector.

bands.K–2: Tell the person who gave you materials honestly that the project did not work.
bands.3–5: Write an honest report that a project failed and what was learned.
bands.6–8: Write a failure report for a described programme that you would actually send, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a failure report you would actually send.
bands.11–12: Write and send a real failure report to a real donor, and record the response.

themes.theme: Audit and what it looks for
themes.description: What an audit looks for, and preparing without theatre.

bands.K–2: Keep the receipts for a class purchase so an adult can check them.
bands.3–5: Prepare the records for a school project so someone could check every spend.
bands.6–8: Prepare one audit trail for a described project and have it tested, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Prepare one audit trail and have it tested.
bands.11–12: Prepare a real audit trail, have it tested by an auditor, and fix what it found.

themes.description: Procurement under time pressure, and the controls that must not be dropped.

bands.K–2: Say which checks you must still do when buying something in a rush.
bands.3–5: List the checks that must not be skipped when a school buys something urgently.
bands.6–8: Identify the procurement controls that survive an emergency and those that do not, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify the controls that survive an emergency and those that do not.
bands.11–12: Identify the controls for a real emergency procurement, apply them, and document the ones that were dropped and why.

themes.description: Closing a programme well, which takes longer than anybody budgets.

bands.K–2: Plan how to end a class project properly, and notice it takes longer than you think.
bands.3–5: Make a closure plan for a school project with a realistic timeline.
bands.6–8: Produce a closure plan for a described programme with a realistic timeline, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce a closure plan with a realistic timeline.
bands.11–12: Produce and run a closure plan for a real programme, and record how long it actually took.

themes.theme: Duty of care to national staff
themes.description: Duty of care to national staff, who carry the most risk and receive the least.

bands.K–2: Say whether everyone helping gets the same care, and whether that is fair.
bands.3–5: Compare how a story organisation treats its local and its visiting staff.
bands.6–8: Compare the provisions for national and international staff in one described organisation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Compare the provisions for national and international staff in one organisation.
bands.11–12: Compare the provisions in a real organisation and put the gap to the people who set them.

themes.description: Security as a decision the team shares rather than one imposed from a capital.

bands.K–2: Let the people doing a risky job help decide how to do it safely.
bands.3–5: Run a safety decision for a school trip with the people going on it.
bands.6–8: Run a security decision for a described situation that includes the people bearing the risk, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Run a security decision that includes the people bearing the risk.
bands.11–12: Run a real security decision with the people bearing the risk, and record how it differed from the capital's view.

themes.theme: Stress, and the year after a deployment
themes.description: Stress and the year after a deployment, which is when most of it arrives.

bands.K–2: Say how someone might feel after a hard time is over, and what helps.
bands.3–5: Say what support someone needs three, six and twelve months after a hard job.
bands.6–8: Identify the support available at three, six and twelve months for a described organisation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify the support available at three, six and twelve months.
bands.11–12: Identify the real support at three, six and twelve months in a real organisation and test whether it can be reached.

themes.theme: The evacuation that leaves people behind
themes.description: The evacuation that takes some people and not others, thought about beforehand.

bands.K–2: Say how you would decide who leaves first in an emergency, before it happens.
bands.3–5: Write fair rules for who is evacuated first, and test them on a story.
bands.6–8: Write evacuation criteria in advance and test them against a scenario, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the criteria in advance and test them against a scenario.
bands.11–12: Write real evacuation criteria with the people they cover, test them in an exercise, and record the objections.

themes.description: Recruiting locally and paying properly, and the market distortion argument examined.

bands.K–2: Say why local helpers should be paid fairly.
bands.3–5: Argue both sides of paying local staff more than the local rate, and choose.
bands.6–8: Argue both sides of the local pay question and take a position, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Argue both sides of the local pay question and take a position.
bands.11–12: Argue both sides for a real recruitment, take a position, and set the real rate.

themes.description: Language, translation, and the power held by whoever translates.

bands.K–2: Play a game of passing a message through a translator and see what changed.
bands.3–5: Say what a project loses when only one person can translate.
bands.6–8: Identify what a described programme loses to translation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify what your programme loses to translation.
bands.11–12: Identify what a real programme loses to translation, with its translators, and change one thing.

themes.theme: A team across time zones and cultures
themes.description: A team across time zones and cultures, where the default meeting time is a decision.

bands.K–2: Pick a meeting time for friends in different places so it is fair.
bands.3–5: Redesign a schedule for a team in different countries so the same people do not always pay.
bands.6–8: Redesign a meeting pattern for a described team that does not always cost the same people, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Redesign a meeting pattern that does not always cost the same people.
bands.11–12: Redesign a real team's meeting pattern and record who paid the cost each month afterwards.

themes.description: Whistleblowing inside an agency, the protection claimed and the protection real.

bands.K–2: Say who you would tell if you saw something wrong in a group, and who would protect you.
bands.3–5: Map how to report wrongdoing at school and what protection exists at each step.
bands.6–8: Map the whistleblowing route and the actual protection at each step for a described agency, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map the route and the actual protection at each step.
bands.11–12: Map the real route in a real agency and verify the protection at each step with someone who has used it.

themes.description: Burnout as a structural outcome rather than a personal failure.

bands.K–2: Say what makes people too tired to keep helping, and what a group could change.
bands.3–5: Find what about a job, not the person, makes people burn out.
bands.6–8: Identify the structural drivers of burnout in one described team, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify the structural drivers in one real team.
bands.11–12: Identify the structural drivers in a real team with them, and change one.

themes.description: Why people leave the sector, asked of people who left.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why they left a job they cared about, and listen without arguing.
bands.3–5: Interview someone who left a caring job and write their reasons without defending the job.
bands.6–8: Interview somebody who left the sector and record their account without defending the sector, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Interview somebody who left and record their account without defending the sector.
bands.11–12: Interview several people who left, record their accounts without defence, and present them to the people who recruit.

themes.theme: What international humanitarian law actually requires
themes.description: The core obligations, stated without the acronyms.

bands.K–2: Say the rules that protect people who are not fighting, in your own words.
bands.3–5: State the main rules that protect civilians in war, plainly.
bands.6–8: State the core obligations of international humanitarian law in plain language, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State the core obligations in plain language.
bands.11–12: State the core obligations in plain language to a real audience and answer their questions accurately.

themes.description: Four different legal statuses with four different entitlements.

bands.K–2: Say the difference between someone who moved for work and someone who had to flee.
bands.3–5: Sort story people into refugee, asylum seeker, migrant and displaced, and say why.
bands.6–8: Classify described cases correctly by legal status, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Classify described cases correctly as refugee, asylum seeker, migrant or displaced.
bands.11–12: Classify real or exercise cases correctly and state the entitlements each status carries where you work.

themes.theme: A mandate, and what your agency may do
themes.description: The limits on your own organisation, which are often not known internally.

bands.K–2: Say what a helper is allowed to do and one thing that is not their job.
bands.3–5: State what one organisation is for and one thing it may not do.
bands.6–8: State a described organisation's mandate and one thing outside it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State your organisation's mandate and one thing outside it.
bands.11–12: State a real organisation's mandate, one thing outside it, and a real case where the line was tested.

themes.description: Talking to whoever controls the road, and what may not be traded for access.

bands.K–2: Say how you would ask someone to let you through, and what you would never give them for it.
bands.3–5: Practise asking for permission to reach people in need, and name what you would not trade.
bands.6–8: Identify what is negotiable and what is not in a described access negotiation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify what is negotiable and what is not.
bands.11–12: Identify what is negotiable and what is not for a real negotiation, and rehearse it with the negotiator.

themes.description: Three separate principles routinely collapsed into one.

bands.K–2: Say what it means to help everyone, take no side, and answer to no one who is fighting.
bands.3–5: Give one example each of being neutral, impartial and independent.
bands.6–8: Distinguish the three principles with a real example of each, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Distinguish them with a real example of each.
